subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 12 periods = 480 minutes
Total: 12 periods · 8h 0min

periods.stage_label: Observe and question: why measurement needs a standard unit
periods.activity_description: Students measure the length of a shared surface (desktop or a strip of paper) using their own handspans, record their counts, and compare results across the group. Differences in counts for the same object surface the core problem: body-part units vary from person to person and cannot give a shared, reliable measurement.

roles.role_description: Sets up the measurement task, collects class data on the board, and leads a brief whole-class discussion on why results differ.
Measures the shared surface with their own handspan, records the count, and explains in one sentence why their answer differs from a classmate's.
Compares handspan counts within a small group and reaches a group statement about what makes handspan unreliable as a unit.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the handspan-measurement task and students measure the shared surface individually, recording their count.
Groups compare their counts, discuss why the numbers differ, and agree on a one-sentence group explanation.
Teacher collects all counts on the board; the class observes the spread of numbers for the same object and identifies what varied.
Whole-class discussion draws out the core insight: a measurement needs a number AND a unit, and the unit must be the same for everyone.
Teacher names the two parts of any measurement (number + unit) and signals that the next unit will introduce units that solve this problem.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit launches the chapter's central question — what makes a measurement trustworthy — so spend the opening orienting students to why they are measuring, not just how. Watch for students who think the tallest student's handspan should simply 'win'; the point is not whose unit is biggest but that no body-part unit is stable across people. A useful checkpoint: ask each group to state what would need to be true for all their counts to agree — students who say 'same-sized hand' are ready to move forward.
materials: Strip of paper or tape marking a fixed length on each desk

periods.stage_label: Observe and question: why measurement needs a standard unit
periods.activity_title: SI Units and the Metre Family
periods.activity_description: Building on the handspan problem, students learn the SI system and the metre as the agreed standard unit for length, along with its sub-units (cm, mm) and the larger unit km. They construct and record the four unit-conversion relationships and locate the smallest graduation on a school scale.

roles.role_description: Explains the historical need for a common system, introduces SI units, and guides students through the unit-conversion relationships with concrete referents.
Records the conversion relationships in a structured table and identifies the smallest graduation on their own school scale.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the previous unit's finding and explains how different measurement systems across regions created confusion, leading countries to agree on SI units.
Teacher introduces the metre, centimetre, millimetre, and kilometre with everyday referents (door width ≈ 1 m; thumbnail width ≈ 1 cm) and writes the four conversion relationships on the board.
Students copy the conversion table, then examine their 15-cm school scale to locate and record the smallest graduation (1 mm) and count the number of cm divisions.
Teacher mentions the Indian historical context — angula, dhanusa, yojana — and students discuss one situation from daily life where each of mm, cm, m, and km is the most appropriate unit.
Quick oral round: teacher names an object, students call out the best unit — consolidating unit-selection before the next unit on technique.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established why a standard is needed; this unit delivers the SI solution, so connect those two moves explicitly at the start. A common confusion is treating centimetre and millimetre as interchangeable for small objects — stress that mm is the smallest graduation on their scale, not the smallest possible measurement. The oral round at the close doubles as a readiness check: students who hesitate on km vs m need a quick nudge before the technique unit begins.

periods.stage_label: Classify and apply: correct technique and the right instrument
periods.activity_title: Measuring Right: Placement, Eye Position, and the Broken Scale
periods.activity_description: Students practise the three correct-technique rules — flat placement, vertical eye position (eliminating parallax), and using a non-zero starting mark — by measuring a pencil, eraser, and comb and recording readings taken from correct and deliberately angled eye positions to observe and explain the difference.

roles.role_description: Demonstrates each technique rule using a large demonstration scale or projected image, then circulates to check student placement and eye position.
Take turns measuring three objects, recording one reading from the correct eye position and one from an angled position, then explaining the discrepancy in writing.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates correct scale placement (flat, zero at one end) and shows what a parallax error looks like when the eye is not directly above the tip.
Groups measure a pencil and eraser using both correct and angled eye positions, recording all four readings and noting which is larger.
Teacher demonstrates the broken-scale technique: starting at a full-centimetre mark and computing length as a difference; groups then apply this to measure a comb starting from the 1-cm mark.
Groups compare their pencil readings across the class; small remaining differences are discussed as residual variation from technique, not unit size.
Teacher poses a closing question: 'Which object in this room could NOT be measured with your 15-cm scale alone?' — setting up the next unit on curved measurement.

periods.teacher_notes: Students come in knowing what a ruler is; the goal here is upgrading how precisely they use one, so frame this as skill-building, not revision. The most common error is reading the scale at an angle and not noticing — pairing students so one measures while the other checks eye position helps catch this immediately. Students are ready to move on when they can correctly compute a broken-scale length without being prompted.
materials: Pencil, eraser, comb (one set per group)

periods.stage_label: Classify and apply: correct technique and the right instrument
periods.activity_title: Measuring What a Scale Cannot Follow: Curved Lengths
periods.activity_description: Students investigate how to measure the length of a curved line — a wavy pencil-drawn curve on paper — using a thread laid along the curve and then straightened against a scale, and compare this to the inadequacy of placing a rigid scale directly on the curve.

roles.role_description: Poses the problem of measuring a curved line, guides groups to propose and test their own methods, and consolidates the thread-and-scale method.
Draw a wavy curve of their own design, attempt to measure it with a rigid scale, then use a thread to measure the same curve and record both results with a written explanation of the difference.

time_bands.activity: Building on the closing question from the previous unit, teacher poses: 'How would you measure the length of a curved line?' and groups briefly discuss and propose methods.
Each group draws a wavy curve on paper and attempts to measure it with their rigid scale; they record what goes wrong and why.
Groups lay a thread carefully along their curve, mark the thread at the curve's end, straighten it, and measure against the scale — recording the curved length.
Groups share their thread-measured lengths and discuss: could a flexible measuring tape do the same job? Teacher connects this to measuring tree girth and body measurements.
Teacher summarises: instrument choice depends on what is being measured — rigid scale for straight, thread or flexible tape for curved — closing Stage 2.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit built straight-line technique; this unit extends the question to curved surfaces, so begin by recalling the closing question from that unit. Students often underestimate how much error comes from placing a thread carelessly — encourage them to pin or hold the thread in place as they go. A good check for readiness is whether students can explain instrument choice (not just perform it): 'Why can't I use a rigid scale here?' should get a causal answer.
materials: Paper and pencil for drawing curves

periods.stage_label: Explain and contextualise: reference points and relative position
periods.activity_title: Where Are You? Discovering the Reference Point
periods.activity_description: Groups of students each stand in different corners of the classroom and measure the distance to a common object (a book on the teacher's desk) from their own positions, then compare distances. The disagreement maps onto Deepa's garden-vs-school dilemma and reveals that distance comparisons require a shared reference point.

roles.role_description: Orchestrates the activity, collects the conflicting distance reports, and guides the class to articulate what was missing — a common fixed reference point.
Measure the distance from their group's corner to the shared object, record it, and then attempt to decide which group is 'closer' — discovering that the answer depends on where you measure from.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the Deepa-and-friends scenario: each child measures from their own house and gets a different answer for which landmark is closer; class discusses what is confusing about this.
Groups measure from their corner to the shared object on the teacher's desk using a metre tape; each group records their distance and reports to the class.
Teacher collects all distances on the board and asks: 'Which group is closest to the book?' — the class discovers the answer depends on which group's starting point is used.
Class agrees on one fixed point (e.g., the door) as the reference, everyone remeasures from that point, and the results now agree on which group's corner is closest.
Teacher introduces the term 'reference point' formally and connects it to kilometre-stone examples on roads; students record a one-sentence definition.

periods.teacher_notes: The measurement skills built in the previous two units are the tool here; the new concept is that distance has no meaning without a fixed origin, which is a genuine conceptual shift. Watch for students who think any starting point is equally valid as long as it is consistent within one measurement — the point is that comparisons across people or objects require the same reference. The kilometre-stone analogy (distances to Delhi) gives an intuitive real-world anchor for students who remain uncertain.
materials: Chalk or sticker to mark the shared reference point on the floor

periods.stage_label: Explain and contextualise: reference points and relative position
periods.activity_title: Motion or Rest? It Depends on Your Reference
periods.activity_description: Students analyse the scenario of Deepa on the bus: seated passengers appear at rest relative to Deepa but in motion relative to a stationary building outside. Small groups construct two reference-point scenarios of their own — one in which a chosen object is at rest and one in which the same object is in motion — using measurement and position language.

roles.role_description: Presents the bus scenario, asks focused questions to surface the relativity of motion, and ensures students articulate both reference points explicitly in each scenario.
Analyse the bus scenario together, then devise and write two contrasting scenarios (same object, different reference point, opposite motion judgement) using position-change language.

time_bands.activity: Teacher narrates the bus scenario — Deepa sees seated passengers as at rest, a person outside sees them as in motion — and asks: 'Are the passengers moving or not?' Groups discuss.
Class establishes the definition: an object is in motion if its position changes with respect to the reference point with time; at rest if it does not.
Groups devise their own two-scenario pair (same object described as at rest from one reference point, in motion from another) and write it up using the formal definition.
Two or three groups share their scenarios; class checks whether both the reference point and the position-change justification are explicit in each case.
Teacher consolidates: motion and rest are not absolute properties of an object — they depend on the chosen reference point — and signals that the next unit will classify what kinds of motion exist.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit introduced the reference point for measuring position; this unit extends it to the definition of motion, so link those ideas at the start. The dominant misconception to watch for is that 'moving' and 'at rest' are intrinsic to an object — students may insist the bus passengers are obviously moving; press them to name their reference point. Groups that successfully produce two contrasting scenarios with explicit reference points are demonstrating the core insight and are ready for classification.

periods.stage_label: Classify and investigate: types of motion by path
periods.activity_title: Tracing Paths: Linear and Circular Motion
periods.activity_description: Students observe and produce examples of linear and circular motion using simple classroom objects — dropping an eraser (linear) and whirling an eraser on a thread in a horizontal circle (circular, as in Activity 5.4) — then sketch the path of each motion and classify it, explaining what determines the path type.

roles.role_description: Introduces the classification framework (motion classified by path shape), supervises the whirling activity safely, and draws out the contrast between a straight and a circular path.
Perform both demonstrations, sketch the resulting path for each, and write a one-sentence classification justification explaining what makes each path linear or circular.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the idea that motion can be classified by the shape of the path the object traces, and lists linear and circular as the first two types.
Each student drops an eraser from a fixed height and observes its path; groups sketch the path and agree on a one-word description.
Groups tie an eraser to a thread, whirl it horizontally, observe the circular path, and sketch it alongside the linear path — noting the key difference.
Class collates their path sketches; teacher confirms correct classifications and supplies real-world examples: Republic Day march (linear), merry-go-round (circular).
Teacher asks: 'Can you think of a motion where an object goes back and forth rather than straight or in a circle?' — previewing oscillatory motion for the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The concept of motion type is new here; stages 3 and 4 together form the motion half of this chapter, so remind students that the reference-point idea from the previous units is still operating — the path is what the object traces relative to a fixed point. Students sometimes think circular motion means the object itself spins; clarify that it is the path of travel that is circular, not the object's rotation. The preview question at the close is intentional — it activates prior intuition about swings and pendulums before the next unit makes it formal.
materials: Eraser and thread (about 40 cm per group)

periods.stage_label: Classify and investigate: types of motion by path
periods.activity_title: Back and Forth: Investigating Oscillatory Motion
periods.activity_description: Students build a simple pendulum (eraser on thread) and a clamped metal strip (or ruler held at one end), observe and sketch the to-and-fro motion of each, and record what is fixed, what moves, and how the path differs from the circular path they observed in the previous unit.

roles.role_description: Guides construction of the pendulum, demonstrates how to displace it slightly before release, and draws attention to the fixed position the pendulum swings about.
Build the pendulum, observe and sketch its path, compare it to the circular sketch from the previous unit, and classify the motion with a written justification referencing the fixed position.

time_bands.activity: Groups make a pendulum by tying an eraser to a thread and suspending it from a ruler held across two stacks of books; teacher ensures all pendulums are ready.
Students displace the pendulum slightly, release it, observe the to-and-fro motion, and sketch the path — noting that the eraser returns to approximately the same position each swing.
One student holds a ruler firmly at one end on the desk edge while another presses and releases the free end; the class observes and sketches the oscillatory vibration of the ruler.
Groups compare their three path sketches (linear, circular, oscillatory) side by side and write a sentence distinguishing oscillatory from circular motion.
Teacher introduces the 'More to know' note: circular and oscillatory motions are both periodic because the object repeats its path after a fixed interval of time.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit follows directly from the linear and circular unit, completing the three-type classification; begin by displaying the two sketches from the previous unit so students can add their oscillatory sketch to a growing comparison set. A frequent confusion is between circular and oscillatory: students may describe the pendulum as 'going around' — ask them to trace the actual path on paper and they will see it is an arc back and forth, not a full circle. Groups that can articulate 'to and fro about a fixed position' in their own words are ready for the classification activity in the next unit.
materials: Eraser and thread (about 30 cm per group)
Two stacks of books to support the suspension ruler

periods.stage_label: Classify and investigate: types of motion by path
periods.activity_title: Park Observations: Classifying Motion in Context
periods.activity_description: Students examine a described or drawn set of playground equipment — swing, slide, merry-go-round, see-saw, and a child running — and classify each motion as linear, circular, or oscillatory, providing a written justification that names the path and, where applicable, the fixed position or centre.

roles.role_description: Presents the playground scenario (verbally or via a sketch on the board), manages group discussion, and challenges any classification that lacks a path-based justification.
Classify each item of equipment, discuss any disagreements within the group, and produce a written table of equipment, motion type, and justification.

time_bands.activity: Teacher describes or sketches the playground and its equipment on the board; students individually predict the motion type of each item before group discussion begins.
Groups discuss their predictions, resolve disagreements using the path definitions from the previous two units, and fill in a classification table (equipment | motion type | justification).
Each group shares one classification with the class; teacher invites other groups to challenge or confirm, with the rule that any challenge must cite the path definition.
Teacher highlights the see-saw as a potential point of debate (oscillatory, like the pendulum) and the child running as linear, reinforcing why path-based definitions matter.
Students add one object from outside the playground to their table — a ceiling fan, a spinning top — and classify it individually, previewing the next stage's application work.

periods.teacher_notes: The two previous units built the three motion types through direct observation; this unit asks students to classify without performing the motion themselves, which is a step up in abstraction. Watch for students who classify the see-saw as circular because it moves 'in an arc' — the key is whether it returns to a fixed position to-and-fro (oscillatory) or continues around a full circle. The individual extension at the close (ceiling fan, spinning top) is a low-stakes preview of the application thinking required in the final stage.
materials: Blackboard or paper sketch of a playground

periods.stage_label: Apply and integrate: measuring position change to describe and classify motion
periods.activity_description: Student groups are given three unfamiliar motion scenarios — a ball rolling in a straight line, a clock hand moving, and a tuning fork prong vibrating — and must decide: (a) what reference point to choose, (b) how to detect and measure position change over time, and (c) which motion type results. Groups produce a written measurement plan for each scenario.

roles.role_description: Presents the three scenarios, prompts groups to think about what 'measuring position change' means in each case, and circulates to ensure plans reference both measurement technique and motion classification.
Discuss and write a measurement plan for each scenario, specifying reference point, measurement method, expected position-change evidence, and predicted motion type with justification.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the three scenarios and explains that each group must design — not perform — a measurement plan that would let someone else decide the motion type.
Groups work on their three plans, drafting reference point, measurement method, and predicted motion classification for each scenario.
Groups compare plans for the clock-hand scenario; class debates whether the hand shows circular or oscillatory motion and resolves it using the path definition (full circle, not to-and-fro).
Teacher focuses on the tuning fork: students recognise it as oscillatory and link it to the metal-strip activity from Stage 4, connecting back-and-forth vibration to the same definition.
Teacher signals that the final two units will bring measurement technique and motion classification together into a single integrated problem.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit marks the start of the final integration stage, where measurement skill and motion classification must work together — briefly recap that these two capacities have been built separately and now converge. The clock-hand debate is intentionally provocative: students who saw the pendulum as circular will make the same error here, so use it as a teachable moment for path completeness (does it go all the way around, or back and forth?). Plans that specify both a reference point and a measurement method signal readiness; plans that only name the motion type are incomplete.

periods.stage_label: Apply and integrate: measuring position change to describe and classify motion
periods.activity_title: Measure, Record, Classify: A Full Motion Investigation
periods.activity_description: Groups choose one motion type (linear, circular, or oscillatory), set up a simple classroom demonstration of it using available materials, measure a relevant length or displacement using correct scale technique, and produce a written investigation record that links measurement data to the motion classification and the reference point used.

roles.role_description: Approves each group's chosen motion and measurement plan before they begin, then circulates to ensure measurement technique (placement, eye position) is being applied correctly alongside classification reasoning.
Set up their demonstration, carry out measurements using correct technique, record data, classify the motion with a written justification, and identify what reference point they used.

time_bands.activity: Groups present their motion choice and measurement plan to the teacher for a quick approval check; any plans missing the reference point or measurement method are revised before proceeding.

Groups set up and run their demonstration: measuring the string length of a pendulum and the arc it swings through, or the radius of a circular path, or the straight-line distance of a rolling object — recording readings correctly.
Groups write their investigation record: what they set up, what reference point they used, what they measured, the measurement value, and the motion classification with justification.
Teacher does a rapid gallery walk — each group's written record is visible — and flags any record that is missing a reference point or a measurement value for revision in the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the practical heart of the integration stage; students have all the component skills and this is the first time they must deploy them together in a self-chosen context. The most common gap is recording a motion classification without any measurement data — remind groups that the investigation record must contain a number and a unit alongside the path description. The gallery walk at the close is formative: it gives you a picture of which groups are ready and which need targeted support in the final unit.
materials: Eraser and thread (for pendulum or circular motion)
Small ball or book (for linear motion)

periods.stage_label: Apply and integrate: measuring position change to describe and classify motion
periods.activity_title: Presenting Evidence: Motion, Measurement, and the Reference Point
periods.activity_description: Groups present their investigation records from the previous unit to the class, explaining how their measurement of length or displacement, combined with a stated reference point, supports their motion classification. Peers ask one probing question per group; the teacher consolidates by showing how all three motion types and the full measurement toolkit appear across the class's work.

roles.role_description: Facilitates presentations, ensures each group states reference point and measurement data explicitly, and delivers a closing consolidation that maps the class's collective work onto the chapter's two central ideas.
Present their investigation record in brief, field one peer question, and update their written record with any correction or addition that the discussion reveals.
Poses one probing question to each presenting group and notes in their own record one thing their investigation would do differently based on the discussion.

time_bands.activity: Groups present in turn (roughly equal sharing of this band); each presentation states the motion set up, the reference point chosen, the measurement taken (with value and unit), and the classification justification.

After all presentations, teacher maps the class's work on the board: one column per motion type, measurement examples listed under each, showing that position change relative to a reference point defines all three types.
Teacher revisits one or two cases where measurement technique or reference-point specification was incomplete (from the gallery walk) and the class collaboratively corrects them.
Students individually write one sentence that connects accurate measurement with motion classification — the chapter's two central ideas in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit draws the chapter together through student-generated evidence rather than teacher summary, so keep your consolidation targeted rather than comprehensive. Watch for groups that describe motion correctly but omit the measurement value — the final sentence task (connecting measurement to classification) is designed to surface and correct exactly this gap. Students who can write that sentence clearly — linking a number-and-unit measurement to a reference-point-based classification — have reached the chapter's highest-order target.
materials: Groups' investigation records from the previous unit

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and question: why measurement needs a standard unit
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students measure with body-part units to discover why a standard is needed, then learn the SI metre family and unit-conversion relationships.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain why body-part units are unreliable and state the SI unit for length along with its sub-unit and super-unit conversions (mm, cm, m, km).

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify and apply: correct technique and the right instrument
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students practise correct scale technique (placement, eye position, broken-scale reading) and measure curved lengths using a thread, selecting the right instrument for each task.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can measure a straight length correctly (with proper placement, eye position, and broken-scale technique) and measure a curved length using a thread, choosing the appropriate instrument for each type of measurement.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain and contextualise: reference points and relative position
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students discover the need for a shared reference point for distance comparison and apply the definition of motion and rest relative to a chosen reference point.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can define a reference point, explain why distance comparisons require a shared reference, and classify a given object as in motion or at rest with respect to a named reference point.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify and investigate: types of motion by path
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe, produce, sketch, and classify linear, circular, and oscillatory motion through hands-on activities and a playground classification exercise.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify any given motion as linear, circular, or oscillatory by identifying the shape of the path traced and, for oscillatory motion, the fixed position about which the object moves.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Apply and integrate: measuring position change to describe and classify motion
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students design measurement plans, conduct a full investigation using correct scale technique, and present evidence linking measured position change (with reference point) to motion type classification.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can measure length accurately using standard SI units and describe and classify motion by identifying how an object's position changes relative to a stated reference point over time.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and question: why measurement needs a standard unit
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why body-part units are unreliable and state the SI unit for length along with its sub-unit and super-unit conversions (mm, cm, m, km).

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in indigenous, non-standard, and standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: Five students measure the same classroom table using their handspans and get five different counts. Which statement best explains why this happens?

options.label: A
options.text: A handspan is too small a unit to measure a table, so large errors appear.

options.label: B
options.text: Each student counted incorrectly because they were not careful enough.

options.label: C
options.text: The handspan varies from person to person, so the unit itself is not the same for everyone.

options.label: D
options.text: The table changes length slightly depending on temperature.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student attributes measurement variation to human error rather than to the unit itself — they have not grasped that non-standard units are structurally unreliable regardless of care.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses measurement variability with a physical property of the object — a misconception that the object rather than the unit is at fault.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student conflates unit size with unit reliability — they recognise handspan is small but have not understood that the problem is inconsistency, not smallness.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with abstract reasoning about units can be prompted to re-enact the handspan activity before answering. Students who express their thinking orally before choosing an option are equally demonstrating the outcome.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and question: why measurement needs a standard unit
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why body-part units are unreliable and state the SI unit for length along with its sub-unit and super-unit conversions (mm, cm, m, km).

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in indigenous, non-standard, and standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: A student needs to express a length of 2.5 km in metres. Which value is correct?

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student multiplied by 100 instead of 1000 — confusing the km-to-m conversion with the m-to-cm conversion.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student multiplied by 10 000 — a non-standard factor suggesting confusion between multiple conversion steps applied incorrectly in sequence.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student applied the correct km-to-m factor but then wrote the unit as cm, indicating the conversion relationships between units have not been consolidated.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find multi-step unit conversion challenging can be encouraged to write out the conversion chain (1 km = 1000 m) as a visual scaffold before computing. Oral explanation of the reasoning is equally valid evidence.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and apply: correct technique and the right instrument
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can measure a straight length correctly (with proper placement, eye position, and broken-scale technique) and measure a curved length using a thread, choosing the appropriate instrument for each type of measurement.

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in indigenous, non-standard, and standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: A student measures a pencil using a scale whose zero end is chipped. The pencil's left end aligns with the 2.0 cm mark and its right end aligns with the 14.5 cm mark. What is the correct length of the pencil?

options.label: A
options.text: 2.0 cm

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student read the right-end mark directly as the measurement — failing to apply the broken-scale technique of computing a difference.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added the two readings instead of subtracting — a procedural reversal of the correct operation.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student recorded the starting mark as the length — confusing the reference reading with the measurement itself.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the subtraction step can be encouraged to draw the pencil on paper with both marks labelled before computing. Pairing with a peer to physically demonstrate the broken-scale technique is equally valid.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and apply: correct technique and the right instrument
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can measure a straight length correctly (with proper placement, eye position, and broken-scale technique) and measure a curved length using a thread, choosing the appropriate instrument for each type of measurement.

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in indigenous, non-standard, and standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: Anish wants to measure the total length of a curved string-light decoration on an arched verandah. Which method will give the most accurate measurement?

options.label: A
options.text: Estimate the length by comparing it to a known straight object nearby.

options.label: B
options.text: Hold a 15-cm rigid scale flat against the arch and read the length directly.

options.label: C
options.text: Lay a thread carefully along the entire arch, mark the end point, then measure the thread against a metre scale.

options.label: D
options.text: Measure the straight-line distance between the two ends of the arch and record that as the string length.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student defaults to the familiar rigid scale without recognising that it cannot conform to a curved surface — an instrument-selection failure.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student substitutes estimation for measurement — not applying any formal technique from the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student measures the chord rather than the arc — confusing the straight-line distance between endpoints with the actual curved length along the surface.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are unsure can be asked to physically attempt laying a rigid scale on a curved surface before answering. Drawing the arch and the chord on paper helps students who are confused between chord and arc.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and apply: correct technique and the right instrument
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can measure a straight length correctly (with proper placement, eye position, and broken-scale technique) and measure a curved length using a thread, choosing the appropriate instrument for each type of measurement.

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in indigenous, non-standard, and standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: A student measures a pencil with their eye placed to the side of the scale rather than directly above it. Explain what error this causes and state what the student should do instead to measure correctly.
expected_elements: Naming the error as parallax (or describing that the eye's angled position makes the tip appear to align with a different mark than it actually does).
Stating that the recorded length will be different from the actual length (too large or too small, depending on the angle).
Stating the correct action: position the eye directly above the point being measured so the line of sight is perpendicular to the scale.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to write their explanation can be invited to demonstrate the correct and incorrect eye positions physically before writing. Labelled diagrams showing the eye position are equally valid evidence of the understanding.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain and contextualise: reference points and relative position
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can define a reference point, explain why distance comparisons require a shared reference, and classify a given object as in motion or at rest with respect to a named reference point.

competency.competency_text: Describe one-dimensional and path-characterised motion using physical measurements of position.

assessment_items.question_text: Deepa says the school is 500 m from her house. Anish says the school is 300 m away. Both are correct. What is the most likely reason for the difference?

options.label: A
options.text: Distance to a building always varies depending on the weather.

options.label: B
options.text: One of them made a calculation error when measuring.

options.label: C
options.text: The school moved between the two measurements.

options.label: D
options.text: They are measuring from different starting points — their own houses — which are not in the same location.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student attributes the difference to human error — they have not recognised that different reference points produce legitimately different, non-erroneous distances.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student applies impossible physical reasoning to rescue a single fixed distance — they have not understood that distance is measured from a point, not inherent in the object.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student introduces an irrelevant external variable — indicating they have not engaged with the reference-point concept at all.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle can be invited to draw two houses and the school on paper, then draw lines from each house to the school, before answering. Oral explanation of the drawing is equally valid.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain and contextualise: reference points and relative position
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can define a reference point, explain why distance comparisons require a shared reference, and classify a given object as in motion or at rest with respect to a named reference point.

competency.competency_text: Describe one-dimensional and path-characterised motion using physical measurements of position.

assessment_items.question_text: Deepa is sitting inside a moving bus. She observes a fellow passenger seated two rows ahead of her. With respect to Deepa as the reference point, what is the state of the seated passenger?

options.label: A
options.text: At rest, because the passenger's position relative to Deepa is not changing.

options.label: B
options.text: At rest only if the passenger is looking straight ahead.

options.label: C
options.text: In motion, because the bus is moving.

options.label: D
options.text: Sometimes at rest and sometimes in motion depending on the speed of the bus.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student correctly notes the bus is moving but incorrectly assigns that motion to the passenger relative to Deepa — conflating absolute ground-frame motion with relative motion.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student introduces bus speed as a factor that changes the relative state — indicating they have not grasped that the reference point (Deepa) and the passenger move together, keeping relative position constant.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student introduces an irrelevant physical attribute (the passenger's gaze direction) — showing confusion about what determines motion relative to a reference point.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find relative motion abstract can be invited to act out the scenario: two students walk together at the same pace and decide whether one is 'moving' from the other's perspective. This embodied version is equally valid evidence.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain and contextualise: reference points and relative position
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can define a reference point, explain why distance comparisons require a shared reference, and classify a given object as in motion or at rest with respect to a named reference point.

competency.competency_text: Describe one-dimensional and path-characterised motion using physical measurements of position.

assessment_items.question_text: A kilometre stone on the road to Delhi reads '145 km'. Explain what this means and identify the reference point being used.
expected_elements: Stating that 145 km is the distance from the stone's location to Delhi.
Identifying Delhi (or a fixed point in Delhi) as the reference point.
Explaining that this figure only makes sense because all kilometre stones on this road use the same reference point — allowing travellers to compare distances meaningfully.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who have not seen kilometre stones can be invited to describe an equivalent reference-based signage system they are familiar with (directions from a bus stand, for example). Labelled diagrams of the road and reference point are accepted alongside or instead of prose.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and investigate: types of motion by path
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify any given motion as linear, circular, or oscillatory by identifying the shape of the path traced and, for oscillatory motion, the fixed position about which the object moves.

competency.competency_text: Describe one-dimensional and path-characterised motion using physical measurements of position.

assessment_items.question_text: A child on a swing moves to and fro, always returning to pass through the lowest point. What type of motion does the swing show, and what is the key feature that determines this classification?

options.label: A
options.text: Circular motion, because the swing moves along an arc.

options.label: B
options.text: Linear motion, because the swing moves in one direction at a time.

options.label: C
options.text: Oscillatory motion, because the swing is connected to a rope.

options.label: D
options.text: Oscillatory motion, because the swing moves to and fro about a fixed position.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student identifies the arc correctly but equates arc with circular path — the dominant confusion between oscillatory and circular motion in this chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student focuses on one-way travel within a half-swing and ignores the to-and-fro return — missing the defining feature of oscillatory motion.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student selects the correct motion type but gives an irrelevant justification (the rope) — indicating the classification label has been memorised without the path-based criterion being understood.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who confuse arc with circle can physically trace the path on paper — drawing the full arc and then asking whether it closes into a full circle — before answering. Embodied demonstration with arm movement is also accepted.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and investigate: types of motion by path
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify any given motion as linear, circular, or oscillatory by identifying the shape of the path traced and, for oscillatory motion, the fixed position about which the object moves.

competency.competency_text: Describe one-dimensional and path-characterised motion using physical measurements of position.

assessment_items.question_text: Students in a Republic Day parade march in a straight line from one end of the field to the other. Which type of motion does this represent?

options.label: A
options.text: Circular motion, because many students move together in a group.

options.label: B
options.text: Linear motion, because all the students maintain the same speed.

options.label: C
options.text: Linear motion, because the students move along a straight path.

options.label: D
options.text: Oscillatory motion, because the students move back and forth across the field.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student applies oscillatory to group movement — incorrectly inferring back-and-forth from a parade that does not actually return, showing confusion about which observable feature drives classification.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student attributes motion type to the number of objects moving together rather than to the path shape — indicating a fundamental misunderstanding of path-based classification.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student selects the correct type but justifies it by speed rather than path — the classification criterion has not been internalised even though the label is right.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who select the correct answer but cannot explain it can be asked to draw the path of one marcher on paper — the straight line is the observable evidence. Pairing with a peer who can explain the path-based criterion is equally valid.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and investigate: types of motion by path
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify any given motion as linear, circular, or oscillatory by identifying the shape of the path traced and, for oscillatory motion, the fixed position about which the object moves.

competency.competency_text: Describe one-dimensional and path-characterised motion using physical measurements of position.

assessment_items.question_text: A thin metal strip is clamped firmly at one end on the edge of a desk. When the free end is pressed down and released, the strip vibrates. (a) Classify the motion of the free end of the strip. (b) Identify the fixed position about which it moves. (c) Explain how this motion is different from the motion of an eraser whirled on a thread.
expected_elements: Classifying the motion of the free end as oscillatory.
Identifying the clamped end (fixed end) as the fixed position about which the free end moves to and fro.

Explaining the difference: the whirled eraser follows a complete circular path around a centre, while the metal strip's free end moves to and fro — it does not complete a full circle but reverses direction about a fixed point.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find the written comparison difficult can sketch the two paths — the arc of the strip and the full circle of the eraser — side by side as their primary answer. Annotated sketches are valid evidence of the analytical distinction.

assessment_items.stage_label: Apply and integrate: measuring position change to describe and classify motion
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can measure length accurately using standard SI units and describe and classify motion by identifying how an object's position changes relative to a stated reference point over time.

competency.competency_text: Describe one-dimensional and path-characterised motion using physical measurements of position.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Time | Position from wall (cm)
0 s | 20
5 s | 20
10 s | 20

assessment_items.question_text: A student tracks the position of a book on a desk every 5 seconds, measuring its distance from a wall. Refer to the table provided. What can be concluded about the book's motion, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: The book is at rest because it is a heavy object and heavy objects do not move.

options.label: B
options.text: The book is at rest because its position relative to the wall does not change over time.

options.label: C
options.text: The book is in motion because all objects on a desk eventually move.

options.label: D
options.text: The book is in motion because the student measured it four times.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses the act of measuring with evidence of motion — they have not used the position-change criterion to judge state of motion.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student applies a non-scientific intuition (objects eventually move) rather than reading the data — the position values in the table are not being used as evidence.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student reaches the correct conclusion (at rest) but for an incorrect reason (mass) — they are applying the common misconception that heavy objects are inherently stationary rather than using the reference-point definition.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to read the table can be asked to describe in words what they notice about the numbers in the position column before choosing an answer. Oral reasoning from the table values is equally valid evidence.

assessment_items.stage_label: Apply and integrate: measuring position change to describe and classify motion
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can measure length accurately using standard SI units and describe and classify motion by identifying how an object's position changes relative to a stated reference point over time.

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in indigenous, non-standard, and standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: A student wants to measure how far a pendulum swings from its rest position to its farthest point. She places a scale on the table below the pendulum and reads 4.5 cm as the distance. Her partner says the reading is 5.0 cm because he was looking at the scale from the side. Which student is correct, and what error did the other student make?

options.label: A
options.text: Both are correct because different eye positions always give acceptable readings within 1 cm.

options.label: B
options.text: Neither is correct; a scale cannot be used to measure a pendulum's swing at all.

options.label: C
options.text: The first student is correct; reading from the side introduces parallax error, making the reading appear larger than it is.

options.label: D
options.text: The partner is correct; reading from the side gives a wider field of view and more accurate results.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student incorrectly reasons that a wider view improves accuracy — they have not learned that a perpendicular line of sight is required to eliminate parallax.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student overgeneralises — concluding that a scale is the wrong instrument for any motion measurement rather than identifying the technique error.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student introduces a tolerance range to make both readings acceptable — a misconception that measurement variation below a threshold is always legitimate, rather than understanding that parallax is a systematic error.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can physically re-enact the two eye positions with a ruler and an eraser to observe the apparent shift before answering. Explaining the answer through a sketch of the eye, scale, and object is equally valid.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can measure length accurately using standard SI units and describe and classify motion by identifying how an object's position changes relative to a stated reference point over time.

competency.competency_text: Describe one-dimensional and path-characterised motion using physical measurements of position.

assessment_items.question_text: A student sets up a pendulum using an eraser on a thread. She states: 'The eraser is always at rest because it keeps returning to the same position.' Evaluate this claim. In your response: (a) identify what is correct and what is incorrect in the student's reasoning, (b) use the definition of motion with reference to a reference point, and (c) state which type of motion the pendulum shows and why.
look_for: The student explicitly identifies what is correct in the claim: the eraser does return to (approximately) the same lowest point, which is a true observation.

The student identifies the error: returning to the same position periodically does not mean the eraser is always at rest — between returns, its position relative to the fixed support point is changing, so it is in motion during the swing.

The student applies the formal definition: an object is in motion when its position changes relative to a reference point over time; the eraser's position changes relative to the fixed support during each swing.
The student correctly classifies the motion as oscillatory and justifies this by the to-and-fro path about a fixed position (the lowest point or the fixed support).
The response uses measurement or position-change language (not just labels), showing integration of both central ideas.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find extended writing difficult can be invited to annotate a diagram of the pendulum — marking the reference point, the path, and the direction of position change at different moments — and write one sentence per point. Diagrams with labels are valid evidence of the integrated reasoning.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Object | Reference point | Measured length/distance (cm) | Does position change over time? | Motion type | Justification (path + reference point)
Eraser dropped from a fixed height | Top of drop point | | | |
Eraser tied to thread, whirled horizontally | Centre of the circle | | | |
Pendulum (eraser on thread) at its lowest point | Fixed support above | | | |
A book resting on a desk | Nearest wall | | | |
assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. For each object: (1) use a scale or metre tape to measure the relevant length or distance stated in the 'Measured length/distance' column and record it with its unit, (2) decide whether the object's position changes relative to the named reference point over time and record Yes or No, (3) classify the motion type, and (4) write a justification that names the path shape and the reference point. Discuss your completed table with your group and resolve any disagreements using the definitions from this chapter.
assessment_items.scaffold: Before filling in the table: for each row, ask yourself — 'What path does this object trace?' and 'Does its distance from the reference point change as it moves?' Use these two questions to guide your measurement choice and your justification.
format_of_output: Completed table with all five columns filled for each row
One group sentence at the bottom of the table: 'The motion type is determined by ___ and measured using ___.'

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: This format requires students to simultaneously apply measurement technique and motion classification with explicit reference points across four contrasting cases — directly demonstrating the chapter's convergent co-central implied LO.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can integrate accurate measurement of length in standard SI units with the reference-point-based definition of motion and path-based classification — the two central operations of this chapter working together.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold questions ('What path does this object trace?' and 'Does its distance from the reference point change?') are designed to activate the two definitions independently before students synthesise them in the justification column. A student who uses only one question is partially integrating; a student who uses both is demonstrating full convergence.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: measured values include a number AND a unit; justifications name a specific path shape AND the reference point by name; the book row is correctly classified as at rest with a position-change value of zero. Weak responses: motion type label is given without a path-based justification; measurement column contains a number but no unit; the pendulum's lowest-point position is confused with a state of rest.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with writing justifications can complete the table orally with a peer recording their reasoning. Students with motor difficulties can be supported to mark their measurements on paper strips rather than record numbers. The group sentence at the close can be composed collaboratively and counted as evidence for any individual who finds independent writing difficult.
